Ka Ora Telecare, a national after-hours telehealth service for rural Aotearoa New Zealand: a descriptive cross-sectional evaluation with particular attention to equity of access and outcomes
nodes.venue: Journal of Primary Health Care
nodes.abstract: Introduction Rural communities in Aotearoa New Zealand have reduced access to primary care, particularly after hours, with greater impact on Māori, Pacific peoples and those in areas of higher deprivation. Ka Ora Telecare is a national after-hours telehealth service established to address these gaps without replacing local services. Aim This study aims to describe service use and clinical outcomes for Ka Ora, with attention to rurality, ethnicity and socioeconomic position. Methods A cross-sectional descriptive evaluation of routinely collected, de-identified, aggregated service data, with the consultation as the unit of analysis, was performed. Variables were ethnicity (prioritised), age band, Community Services Card status, deprivation quintile, rurality by the Geographical Classification for Health (GCH), provider type and clinical outcome. Analysis was descriptive. Results Across the 24 month study period, 69,337 consultations carried a valid GCH code: 63.1% in R1 (rural, close to an urban centre), 27.1% in R2 and 5.6% in R3. Māori representation fell from 22.5% in R1 to 16.8% in R3, and Pacific from 3.8% to 1.1%. Of 16,369 clinician-led consultations, 88% were resolved or partially resolved via telehealth and 8% required same-day escalation. Outcomes were similar across ethnic groups, and Māori and Pacific use was concentrated in higher deprivation quintiles. Discussion Ka Ora is functioning as a useful component of the rural primary care system, reaching higher-deprivation populations. Use is concentrated in less remote rural communities, and Māori and Pacific representation declines with remoteness even though Māori form a larger share of the population in more remote areas. Whether use is proportionate to need cannot be determined from service-level data.

nodes.name: Geographical indication adoption and county employment dynamics in China: stacked DID evidence on rural-urban and regional heterogeneity
nodes.venue: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
nodes.abstract: Geographical indications (GIs) are widely promoted as place-based institutions that can strengthen rural economies. Yet existing evidence is mixed on whether GI benefits translate into broad-based local employment gains, and whether impacts differ across regions with unequal market access and factor mobility. Using a county-year panel for China spanning 2000–2023 and three overlapping GI channels (protected products, agricultural GI registration, and trademark registration), we estimate dynamic employment responses to GI adoption with stacked difference-in-differences designs that address staggered treatment timing. Rural employment rates rise following GI adoption and remain higher several years after designation, whereas urban employment effects are smaller and more heterogeneous. Macro-regional analyses indicate that rural gains are concentrated in Western China, while Central China exhibits weak or negative rural responses at longer horizons. For urban employment, estimates are imprecise in the East and Central regions and turn negative in the West at 5-year horizons. Province-level results reinforce substantial heterogeneity but are sensitive to treated support and inference limitations. The findings clarify when and where GIs function as effective rural development instruments and motivate more place-sensitive GI governance that complements certification with market access, processing capacity, and local labor demand.

nodes.name: Digital Transformation in Healthcare: The Impacts of Artificial Intelligence on Healthcare Services and Health Economics
nodes.venue: Algorithmic Transformation: Technological, Managerial, Social, and Economic Dimensions of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization
nodes.abstract: Digital transformation in healthcare, driven by the widespread adoption of electronic health records, the growth of large-scale health data, the expansion of telehealth applications, and advances in data-processing capacity, is strengthening the role of artificial intelligence within healthcare systems. Technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative artificial intelligence are increasingly used in diagnosis and screening, clinical decision support, personalized care, patient monitoring, workflow optimization, and the improvement of access to healthcare services. This chapter provides a comprehensive conceptual and narrative review of the effects of artificial intelligence on healthcare services and health economics. It examines the impact of AI on diagnostic accuracy, early detection, clinical decision-making, healthcare professionals’ workload, service capacity, workforce productivity, access, and equity. In addition, the economic value of AI applications is evaluated in terms of cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit, resource allocation, reimbursement mechanisms, health technology assessment, and implementation costs. Existing evidence indicates that AI can accelerate diagnostic processes, reduce unnecessary procedures and tests, improve the utilization of healthcare professionals and high-cost medical equipment, and generate cost-effective outcomes in specific applications. However, the economic value of AI is not uniform across healthcare systems or areas of application. Patient volume, workforce costs, existing infrastructure, licensing and integration expenses, maintenance and updating costs, reimbursement structures, and institutional characteristics of healthcare systems substantially influence economic outcomes. Ethical and regulatory issues, including data security, algorithmic bias, explainability, clinical accountability, human oversight, and equity in access to healthcare, are also critical to the sustainable adoption of AI technologies. Overall, the value of artificial intelligence in healthcare should not be assessed solely on the basis of technical performance or short-term cost savings. A comprehensive assessment should consider clinical outcomes, economic value, implementation conditions, human–AI collaboration, ethical responsibilities, and long-term sustainability together.

Deep Learning and Artificial Intelligence: Conceptual Foundations of Pattern Recognition and Security Applications
nodes.venue: Algorithmic Transformation: Technological, Managerial, Social, and Economic Dimensions of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization
nodes.abstract: The rapid growth of digital data and the increasing complexity of security threats have expanded the use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in modern security systems. This chapter presents the conceptual foundations of deep learning and pattern recognition and examines their roles in security-oriented applications. It first clarifies the relationships among artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and pattern recognition, emphasizing the transition from manually engineered features to representation learning through multilayer neural networks. Fundamental mechanisms of deep learning, including artificial neurons, activation functions, forward propagation, backpropagation, loss functions, and hierarchical representation learning, are subsequently discussed. The chapter also reviews major deep learning architectures, including Multilayer Perceptrons, Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, Autoencoders, and Transformers, with particular attention to their suitability for different data types and security problems. Their applications are examined in the context of intrusion detection, anomaly detection, malware detection, phishing detection, security log analysis, and physical and biometric security. Recent developments involving large language models, federated learning, Edge AI, and continual learning are also considered as emerging directions for security analysis. Beyond predictive performance, the chapter emphasizes that reliable artificial intelligence-based security systems must address several limitations and risks. These include data quality and representativeness, class imbalance, overfitting, data and concept drift, adversarial attacks, data poisoning, model extraction, and membership inference attacks. The discussion further highlights the importance of explainability, privacy, algorithmic fairness, robustness, and human oversight, particularly in high-risk security environments where incorrect decisions may have significant consequences. Overall, the chapter argues that artificial intelligence and security have a bidirectional relationship: artificial intelligence can strengthen threat detection and decision support, while AI systems themselves may become targets of malicious manipulation. Future security systems are therefore expected to rely increasingly on trustworthy, explainable, privacy-aware, adaptive, and human-supervised approaches that combine advanced pattern recognition capabilities with operational and ethical safeguards.

nodes.name: Cognitive-congestion language profiling in ADHD: lexical signal auditing and negative-manifold specificity testing
nodes.venue: Journal of High School Science
nodes.abstract: High machine-learning accuracy in classifying ADHD-related writing does not necessarily establish an ADHD-specific linguistic phenotype, as predictions may reflect diagnostic vocabulary, medication references, or community-specific topics rather than cognitive organization. This study evaluated an interpretable cognitive-congestion language profile (LCCI) and a negative-signature framework for detecting disorder-specific linguistic distinctiveness. A dataset of 25,000 Reddit-derived posts from ADHD, OCD, depression, PTSD, and Asperger/autism-related communities was analyzed using condition-name masking and author-grouped cross-validation. Twenty-five features measuring discourse structure, uncertainty, urgency, lexical diversity, and coherence were compared with TF-IDF classification. The equal-weight LCCI composite performed near chance (ROC-AUC 0.506), while the multivariable profile achieved ROC-AUC 0.654, increasing to 0.681 with learned weights. Individual feature differences were small. TF-IDF substantially outperformed LCCI (ROC-AUC 0.940), with negligible improvement from combining them. An audit classified 59 of 60 high-weight TF-IDF coefficients (98.3%) as topic-related, without quantifying their contribution to predictive performance. To test specificity independently of supervised classification, the negative-signature framework excluded each psychiatric community in turn, constructed a reference language manifold from the remaining communities, and measured residual distinctiveness using PCA reconstruction, shrinkage Mahalanobis distance, and isolation forest. ADHD exhibited no positive residual signal (ROC-AUC 0.451, 0.419, and 0.429, respectively), while OCD showed the greatest residual separability. These findings distinguish predictive discrimination, interpretable linguistic association, and disorder specificity. The principal contribution is a reproducible, generalizable falsification framework demonstrating that strong supervised classification does not establish an ADHD-specific linguistic phenotype and providing a means to evaluate candidate linguistic biomarkers before clinical translation.

nodes.name: Benefits of future satellite gravimetry missions for characterizing extreme wet events in terrestrial water storage
nodes.venue: GRACE/GRACE-FO Science Team Meeting 2026
nodes.abstract: Under the assumption that a warming climate leads to an intensification of the global water cycle, it is hypothesized that also the occurrence frequency and severity of extreme events such as droughts and floods will increase in the upcoming decades. GRACE/-FO observations of terrestrial water storage (TWS) have been used in the past to identify and analyse extreme events both on a global and regional scale. However, these analyses are restricted by the limited spatial and temporal resolution of current satellite gravimetry observations. Especially, flooding events tend to occur very locally and with short temporal (sub-monthly) extent, thus capturing them is challenging. Future satellite gravimetry missions, particularly the double-pair constellation MAGIC, are expected to significantly enhance the spatial and temporal resolution. In this study, we globally investigate the benefit MAGIC can achieve to detect wet extreme events using long-term (50 years) end-to-end simulations of GRACE-C and MAGIC.The simulation environment is based on the acceleration approach and considers tidal and non-tidal background model errors as well as instrument noise of the acceleration and ranging instruments following the current MAGIC mission design studies. As input and reference, we use the daily output of a climate model (GFDL-CM4) from the CMIP6 archive that has been identified as a realistic representation of water storage evolution in previous studies. To explore the improved temporal and spatial resolution expected from the MAGIC constellation, we (i) compare extreme values derived from 5-daily gravity field simulations to those from monthly fields, and (ii) show how the weaker spatial filtering required for MAGIC has a positive influence on the detectability of extremes.For the analysis two different approaches are exploited: One method focuses solely on the stochastic characteristics of the time series in terms of extreme value theory, evaluating the magnitude-frequency relationship of large TWS values by calculating expected return levels of wet extremes. The other approach builds on the fact that a 50-years simulation time series allows to derive statistically meaningful conclusions from directly comparing reference and simulation output on a time series level. We evaluate the time of occurrence of wet extremes on the basis of classification scores assessing correctly and incorrectly identified extreme events.

nodes.name: A Cloud-Computing and AI-Powered Hybrid Deep Learning Approach for Improved Malware Detection
nodes.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics AI-Enabled Enterprise Architecture for Sustainable Universities
nodes.abstract: Although conveniences have accelerated due to the rapid growth of the internet and computer systems, ways to perpetrate cybercrimes have also been on the rise, particularly visible in the continuous malware attacks. This study takes a combined cloud computing and artificial intelligence methods to provide a hybrid deep learning-based architecture for the improvement of malware detection. For substantial classification from CNNs through feature extraction, the proposal contains transfer learning, adversarial training and ensemble methods. It is assured by standardizing the data from network traffic logs social data sets from EICAR and the public viral dataset archives. The experimental results on the Malimg dataset showed 97.8% accuracy which exceeded the accuracy of AlexNet and ResNet-50. The proposal shows a way of improving cybersecurity with some new and hybrid scalable and robust methods.

geofm-landslide-benchmark: cross-model evaluation protocol and derived datasets for geospatial foundation models in landslide susceptibility
nodes.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
nodes.abstract: Reproducibility package for 'What survives an audit: evaluating geospatial foundation models for landslide susceptibility against a geomorphometric baseline' (in preparation for Earth Science Informatics). The code (tag v1.4.0) implements the cross-model benchmark of TerraMind and Prithvi-EO-2.0 against a 17-layer geomorphometric baseline under spatial-block cross-validation, with the random-initialization ablation, point-probe controls (context-matched manual baselines, spectral scar probe, constrained-negative sensitivity), the control arms (ground motion, movement typology, geology, climate), and the audit re-analyses (positional floor on the benchmark folds for every pipeline, range of spatial dependence against the block size, variance of the negative draw and of the block-grid placement, readers tuned by nested spatial cross-validation), together with the table and figure generators and the per-fold result files (JSON) behind every reported number. The deposit adds the derived datasets: 17-layer geomorphometric feature stacks (npz) for five Chilean basins, annual 2023 Sentinel-2 L2A composites (GeoTIFF) built per MGRS tile for Huasco, Maipo and Maule, the sampled benchmark points with spatial-block ids (CSV), the Prithvi input patches of those points (uint16 memmaps) and the Maule fold indices. data/ZENODO_DEPOSIT.md documents every file. The transformer-block sweep, low-rank adaptation, the pre-/post-event test and the Prithvi susceptibility surfaces predate the Prithvi input-offset correction; their result files are kept in the code for traceability but are not reported.
